title: S. Korea sends 2nd relief team to Nepal as 9 nationals remain missing - The Korea Herald
description: S. Korea sends 2nd relief team to Nepal as 9 nationals remain missing  The Korea Herald
publisher.title: The Korea Herald
full_article:
Members of South Korea's Korea Disaster Relief Team load relief supplies onto a KC-330 military transport aircraft at Gimhae Airport on Friday before departing for Nepal to support flood relief efforts. (Foreign Ministry)

South Korea sent a second disaster relief team to Nepal on Friday, carrying about 4 tons of humanitarian supplies. Nine South Koreans remain missing more than two weeks after devastating floods and landslides struck the country.

The eight-member Korea Disaster Relief Team departed from Gimhae Airport at 2:55 a.m. aboard an Air Force KC-330 military transport aircraft and was scheduled to arrive in Kathmandu at around 9 a.m., according to the Foreign Ministry.

The team comprises two officials each from the Foreign Ministry, the National Fire Agency and the Korea International Cooperation Agency, as well as two medical personnel. It will remain in Nepal for seven days.

Unlike the first 44-member contingent, which was largely focused on search-and-rescue operations, the second team will support reconstruction and recovery efforts as the Nepali government shifts its disaster response toward recovery. It will also continue supporting efforts to locate the missing South Koreans.

The aircraft carried about 4 tons of relief supplies worth 180 million won ($134,000), including blankets, winter clothing and tents donated by South Korean companies through nongovernmental organizations.

Meanwhile, the first KDRT contingent is scheduled to leave Nepal on Friday after completing its 10-day mission and arrive in South Korea on Saturday morning.

The 44-member team, including 37 firefighters, had conducted searches using drones, helicopters and other equipment in areas hit by the disaster.

Despite the operation, no trace of the nine missing South Koreans has been found.

The nine — six employees of Doosan Enerbility and three of Korea South-East Power — went missing on Aug. 26 while working at the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower plant construction site in Rasuwa District near the Nepal-Tibet border.

The Foreign Ministry said search efforts would continue even after the first KDRT team leaves, with the second contingent working alongside South Korean government personnel remaining in Nepal, the South Korean Embassy, local authorities and corporate search teams.

A ministry official said large-scale search operations had become increasingly difficult due to the mountainous terrain, weather-related risks and concerns over infectious diseases.

“Despite the difficulties, we will continue search-and-rescue efforts,” the official said.

CHAMONIX-MONT-BLANC, France (AP) — For centuries, French and Italian mountain communities on the flanks of Western Europe’s highest peak have gazed upon seemingly eternal glaciers and snow that gave the colossus its name: Mont Blanc, the white mountain.

But climate warming is dismantling the picture at alarming speed.

Europe’s record heat waves this summer savaged permafrost that for millennia has acted like glue on the Alpine landscape. Defrosting cliffs came apart as high-altitude cold gave way to higher temperatures, sending rock falls cascading from the heights. A famously dangerous rock-prone gully that climbers have long braved on ascents to the summit, 15,766 feet up, became temporarily impassable.

“We weep for our mountain, the way it’s changing. It hits us in the gut,” said Stéphane Bozon, a deputy mayor in Chamonix-Mont-Blanc, a French town at the foot of the giant that straddles France’s border with Italy.

“From mid-July onward, we saw an increase in rock falls. We saw areas becoming difficult to access because of glacial retreat and snowmelt on the glaciers, with crevasses opening up and rock collapses making some areas difficult to reach or traverse,” he told The Associated Press.

Each degree of warming can have an outsized impact. On the Aiguille du Midi peak, which rises to an altitude of 12,605 feet in the Mont Blanc range, average temperatures for July have soared. The Aug. 26 floods that swept through Nepal and China were triggered after a collapse of bedrock and glacier ice sent debris and water surging through multiple Himalayan rivers. Initial assessments of many scientists are that climate change played a key role in creating conditions for the catastrophe.

As Earth’s global average temperature rises because of the burning of oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase.

In the Alps, glaciers once admired for their icy majesty are being eyed with trepidation.

Bozon, who is in charge of safety for Chamonix, says his town urgently needs to prepare for “serious scenarios” of chunks of glacier or mountain potentially falling onto inhabited areas.

“We have to move quite quickly because this summer has shaken us and year after year we’re being shaken by the glaciers’ retreat,” he said.

title: Nepal floods: Suhas Subramanyam joins vigil as seven Loudoun County residents remain missing - Firstpost
description: Nepal floods: Suhas Subramanyam joins vigil as seven Loudoun County residents remain missing  Firstpost
publisher.title: Firstpost
full_article:
Residents of Northern Virginia gathered at South Riding Town Green for an interfaith vigil to mourn those killed in the devastating floods in Nepal and support families still waiting for information about missing relatives.

The gathering brought together local residents, religious leaders, law enforcement officials and elected representatives, including US Congressman Suhas Subramanyam. People held candles, carried photographs of missing community members and observed moments of silence and prayer in memory of those affected by the disaster.

For families with relatives still unaccounted for, the vigil also offered a space to come together as they wait for updates on ongoing search and rescue efforts.

Advertisement

At least seven Loudoun County residents missing

Subramanyam, who represents Virginia's 10th Congressional District, said several of the missing people were from Loudoun County and were known to him personally.

He said the lack of information had made the situation particularly difficult for families who have been left without closure.

Local organisers said at least seven Loudoun County residents remain unaccounted for following the floods. Community representatives have been holding nightly coordination calls to exchange information and support affected families.

Subramanyam said his office has been in regular contact with the US Department of State and emergency response agencies over the rescue efforts.

More from World

He also said the US Department of Defense had sent military aircraft carrying specialised search-and-rescue equipment to support recovery operations in Nepal. Officials are also working on collecting DNA samples from relatives to help identify victims who may be recovered.

Community comes together

Loudoun County law enforcement officials also attended the vigil and expressed their support for families affected by the disaster.

The Loudoun County Sheriff told those gathered that the turnout reflected the community's commitment to supporting one another and continuing efforts to help those affected.

The vigil included prayers from different faith communities and periods of silence as residents remembered the victims and those still missing.

Catastrophic floods triggered by a glacial collapse in Nepal in late August 2026 swelled the Gandak river system flowing towards neighbouring India, prompting authorities in eastern Bihar to open all 36 gates of the Gandak barrage on August 26-27. But footage shared online does not show water being discharged from the barrage, contrary to the circulating claims. The person who filmed the footage told AFP it was recorded months earlier at a different dam in India's western Maharashtra state.

"This is the Gandak barrage in India's Bihar to control water from the massive floods caused by the collapse of glaciers in Nepal as they enter India through the Trishuli, Narayani, and Gandak river system," reads part of a Sinhala-language Facebook post shared on August 29, 2026.

The video shows a drone view of water flowing through the sluice gates of a massive dam.

"This video shows the Yesaji Kank reservoir, also known as Bhatghar dam," Gaikwad told AFP on September 7.

The death toll from the flash floods in Nepal rose to 1,385 on Friday as more bodies were recovered from affected districts, while search and rescue operations continued for more than 5,000 missing people. The floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 and devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

Authorities said the scale of the disaster remained severe, with thousands still unaccounted for and rescue teams continuing their efforts. So far, 13,676 people have been rescued from different areas, while the number of missing people is estimated at 5,130.

Two victims of the flash floods also died in Kathmandu while undergoing treatment.

The joint command of security personnel has continued search and rescue operations across the affected regions. title: Floods and landslides on Nepal-China border kill 1,428 people - UA.NEWS
description: Floods and landslides on Nepal-China border kill 1,428 people  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
As a result of flash floods and landslides on the border between Nepal and China, 1,428 people have died, while another 5,649 are considered missing. Search operations have continued for more than two weeks after the disaster, Anadolu Agency reports.

Losses in Nepal and Tibet

Nepal has confirmed the deaths of 1,385 people, while 5,130 people are still being sought, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said. In China’s Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet, the death toll stands at 43, with another 519 people missing.

Among those missing are 848 foreigners: 587 people are being sought in Nepal and 261 in Tibet.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

How the disaster occurred

The disaster occurred on August 26 after a crack formed in a glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal at an altitude of about 5,200 meters. This triggered an avalanche of ice and rocks that turned into a large-scale debris flow and moved through valleys along the border.

Floods and landslides caused destruction in Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as in the Kathmandu Valley. In Tibet, the disaster buried the Gyirong border crossing.

Nepal has become the first country to invoke the emergency procedures of the world’s fund for climate disaster support, testing a mechanism that experts say does not have enough money to respond.

The Himalayan nation sought emergency funding after flash floods, triggered by a glacial lake collapse, killed more than 1,300 people in late August and left thousands missing.

Finance minister Swarnim Wagle estimates the cost of rebuilding at $4-5bn, describing the figure as preliminary. That is roughly 10 per cent of the country's annual GDP, so it cannot do it alone.

"There is not enough money to cover these disasters and people are left alone with those impacts, or governments in poor countries that are already strained have to deal with them," he explains.

The fund holds $822m in total pledges, but only around $350m is currently earmarked for disbursement. Against that, developing countries have already given 180 applications for a combined $2.8bn.

Harjeet Singh, who has worked on the fund’s design for almost two decades, said the scale of Nepal's need had long been predictable.

"We already knew the scale of damage and loss has reached that level and we’ve been saying that this fund doesn't even have a billion dollars," he says. "Nepal's case actually demonstrates it very well."

A study published in the journal Nature in 2024 estimated that developing countries would need $395bn a year by 2025 to cover the cost of climate-driven loss and damage, a figure broadly consistent with estimates from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change of around $400bn annually.

Countries agreed on a global climate finance target of $300bn a year at Cop29 in Baku last year. The target remains far from being met.

Sherman says the board has deliberately chosen to begin disbursing money now as a test phase, rather than waiting years to design a full long-term model first.

"We could choose to launch a pilot phase now with the money that's available, start getting money out the door, test the systems of the secretariat, test the eligibility process," he says.

"Nobody's suggesting it's anywhere near the requirement of the need for developing countries but it's what we have, and that's why the cap is $20m."

open image in gallery {"id":"trigger-autogallery-58265","index":1} Volunteers remove sludge from a classroom at Shree Bagheswori Madhyamik School in Galchhi, Nepal, on 31 August 2026 ( Reuters )

The funding shortfall isn’t confined to one fund. The Green Climate Fund lost $3bn in pledged money when the US withdrew its support.

The UK has separately cut its own climate finance contribution by roughly half in recent months, even as the fund is meant to serve 134 developing countries.

Singh rejects the idea that the shortfall reflects a lack of money in the global economy.

"Let's look at the money going to the wars," he says. "Let's look at the money that has gone for several bailouts in the past. And we also were able to mobilise trillions of dollars to respond to Covid."

An estimated $7trillion a year in direct and indirect subsidies, he adds, goes to fossil-fuel companies worldwide.

"If you look at the global GDP, which has been growing, of course we have money," he argues. "Now, where’s the money? Money is now with those oligarchs and those billionaires, and now a trillionaire. Inequality has increased. Money is there, it's just that it's going in the wrong direction, and that has to be pointed out."

But could Nepal's disaster push wealthier nations to rethink priorities and contribute more towards climate funding ahead of the upcoming UN general assembly and climate talks in Istanbul?

"The environment right now isn’t very favourable for all these funds," Sherman says, adding that a longer-term model for the loss and damage fund is due to be agreed by December, ahead of a fresh replenishment round expected to take one-two years.

“It's unfortunate, but we knew that this was always going to be a scenario. We can't control what happens."

open image in gallery {"id":"trigger-autogallery-58266","index":2} A woman looks at photographs of missing persons outside a morgue in Kathmandu on 9 September 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Nepal's foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, says his country is ”paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create".

Nepal is one of the least developed countries in the world and contributes negligibly to global heating. Yet, it’s one of the most vulnerable to the climate crisis.

Many countries in Nepal’s position have been demanding compensation from the world’s richest countries responsible for the crisis.

Sherman notes that the word “compensation” carries no legal weight in this context.

"The request for compensation is a political one that is not resolved,” he says. “Developed countries have been very clear that for them, supporting loss and damage is not about compensation for losses, nor is it about them being held liable for the impact of climate change."

open image in gallery {"id":"trigger-autogallery-58267","index":3} An excavator clears mud and debris from a road in Devighat, Nepal, on 10 September 2026 ( Reuters )

Experts say the gap between what Nepal needs and what it can get from the loss and damage fund will likely leave it under debt.

The likeliest source of further support is the World Bank, which gives loans rather than grants. Before Nepal, Pakistan was compelled to take billions of dollars in fresh loans on top of existing debt, including $400m to rebuild homes and infrastructure, after floods in 2022 caused $30bn in damage and killed more than 1,700 people.

Sherman says Nepal will likely follow a similar path, taking on sovereign debt as a consequence of an “event that was not of their making".

Singh describes the pattern as "a double injustice", in which countries least responsible for climate change and least prepared for its impacts are forced into debt to recover from disasters linked to it.

Scientists broadly agree that rising temperatures have destabilised glaciers across the Himalayan region for years, although the precise mechanism behind the August collapse – whether the initial failure began in glacial ice or in permafrost and rock – remains under investigation.

Nepal's president, Ramchandra Paudel, has separately made a formal international appeal for "climate justice", while the prime minister, Balendra Shah, is due to raise the matter at the UN general assembly later this month.

full_article:
Nepal on Wednesday appealed for emergency assistance from a UN fund designed to help developing countries cope with the irreversible effects of climate change, as it sought climate justice and floods caused by an August 26 glacier collapse on its border with China’s Tibet Autonomous Region.

Commenting on the gravity of the situation that Nepal is facing, UN Resident Coordinator for Nepal, Lila Pieters Yahia stated:

The devastation Nepal has experienced is an extraordinary, stark illustration of the losses and damages that climate-vulnerable countries are increasingly facing.

Nepal submitted an urgent request to the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). The government’s letter stated that as “a least developed and highly climate-vulnerable mountainous country, Nepal contributes negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions yet continues to bear disproportionate and escalating climate impacts.”

The Fund was established at the 27th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP27) in 2022 and operationalized at the 28th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP28) in 2023. It is designed to help developing countries respond to climate impacts that cannot be avoided or adapted to. Nepal, whose mountainous terrain makes the country susceptible to melting ice and glacial lake outbursts, was a strong advocate for the Fund’s creation.

The floods have affected 84,270 people. According to the latest update from Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 13,656 people have been rescued, 5,130 remain missing, and 1,377 are confirmed dead.

Nepal and the UN have raised $22 million of a flash appeal for $49.6 million launched last week. The appeal aims to provide direct cash assistance, cold-weather shelter materials, portable solar power units, water purification systems, food aid, and emergency mobile clinics to 84,000 people before the end of the year.

Despite the Fund’s purpose of shifting the burden of climate response away from countries that have contributed least to emissions, pledged amounts fall below projected needs. Only $485.77 million has been received of the $822.71 million pledged. To date, the Fund has not disbursed money to any country.

How the Board responds to Nepal’s request will test whether the Fund can play a meaningful role in climate disaster recovery. By using the language of climate justice, Nepal is pressing the international community to share the financial responsibility for loss and damage caused by climate disasters more equitably.

title: Grants, Not Loans: ANPFA, Nepal’s Peasants’ Union, Demands Climate Justice After Deadly Floods - La Via Campesina
description: Grants, Not Loans: ANPFA, Nepal’s Peasants’ Union, Demands Climate Justice After Deadly Floods  La Via Campesina
publisher.title: La Via Campesina
full_article:
On the morning of August 26, 2026, a mass of rock and ice tore loose from the north face of Langtang Lirung in Nepal’s Rasuwa district and plunged roughly 1,200 vertical meters into a tributary valley. The collapse itself generated a seismic shock equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, as per reports. The resulting slurry has been described as a “sediment bomb”. Within minutes that slurry was moving downstream at speeds topping 150 kilometers an hour, rising as much as 80 meters above normal river levels in places. It tore through the Bhotekoshi river basin, crossed into the Tibet region, and reportedly carried debris and some bodies even into India.

The scale of destruction has been staggering.

At the time of writing this piece, more than 1,300 people are confirmed dead, with over 5,500 more still missing on both sides of the border. Identification of the dead has been slow and, in many cases, impossible, since bodies were swept far from where they were lost. More than 80 bridges were destroyed, along with a major highway connecting the region to the Tibetan border, and over a dozen hydropower plants were damaged, knocking out more than a tenth of the country’s electricity generation.

This is not the first time, and unfortunately won’t be the last either.

A similar glacier-linked disaster in 2015 killed around 300 people, and the same river corridor flooded twice more in July 2025 alone, once from a glacial lake outburst that killed at least 9 people and swept away a bridge, and again three weeks later from a separate flood event.

Scientists studying the disaster point to a familiar and worsening pattern. Glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are retreating at an accelerating pace, and as ice disappears, rock faces once frozen in place become exposed to warmer temperatures, rainfall, and repeated freeze-thaw cycles that weaken them further. Permafrost that once held slopes together is also thawing.

Together, these shifts are making sudden, catastrophic slope failures, like the one at Langtang Lirung, more frequent and harder to predict, even in a region long shaped by earthquakes and unstable terrain.

The Impact on Peasant Communities

For the peasant farmers and herders who live along these river valleys, the disaster has meant a slower, harder kind of ruin on top of the initial destruction. The flood affected roughly 84,000 people across 17 municipalities in 6 districts, and these are mostly rural, hill-region municipalities where agriculture supports about two-thirds of the population’s livelihoods.

Farmland along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi corridors was buried under mud and debris, livestock drowned or were swept away, and homes that families had rebuilt after a similar flood the previous year were destroyed a second time, as noted earlier.

For those whose relatives are missing rather than confirmed dead, the damage compounds further. Without a body, a person cannot be legally declared dead, which leaves families unable to access relief payments, transfer land tenancy, or use joint bank accounts, even as they lose the labor and income that person once provided to the household.

Many of these communities depend on subsistence farming with little cushion for a shock of this size, and the loss of a single planting season, let alone a destroyed field or a drowned animal, can take years to recover from.

















La Via Campesina’s member organization the All Nepal Peasants’ Federation (ANPFA) points out that Nepal’s total contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions is a small fraction of one percent, while its farmers, who burn little fuel and rely on manual labor and saved seed, are absorbing the consequences of warming produced almost entirely elsewhere.

ANPFA also warns that the financing on offer for recovery, largely structured as loans, even on favorable terms, simply turns a climate disaster into new sovereign debt for a country that had no hand in causing it. The union therefore demands converting proposed disaster financing from loans into grants, and channeling loss and damage funds as direct reparations to affected communities rather than through government intermediaries.

After sustained pressure from peoples’ movements and civil society, Nepal’s government has echoed part of this climate justice argument on the international stage, framing its request for support not as aid but as a matter of shared responsibility among major emitters, and has formally sought funding from the international mechanism built to help vulnerable countries cope with climate-driven loss and damage. Even so, the sum requested so far is modest against reconstruction costs estimated in the billions of dollars, a gap that has left peasant families skeptical that the compensation, once it arrives, will look much different from the debt they are already being asked to take on.

“ There is a debt, and it runs from the [Global] North to us, not from us to the World Bank. The people to whom it is owed are being buried two hundred at a time, six districts downstream from where they died, by officials who do not know their names.”, writes Pramesh Pokharel of ANPFA in his witness account of the relief and recovery efforts.

Beyond the financing question, ANPFA is also calling for a public inquiry into why hydropower plants, labor camps, and monitoring stations were built inside a valley that had already flooded once before. And they are also calling for hazard monitoring to be rebuilt outside the flood path, with local farmers and herders included as observers rather than treated as passive subjects of such warnings.

On reconstruction and recovery efforts that target farmers and farm households, ANPFA insists that it should be centered on small-scale, peasant agroecological farming rather than large contract operations, along with death registration and compensation rules that work for a family whose relative is missing rather than confirmed dead.

Key Takeaways Kathmandu limited and coordinated foreign SAR teams to prevent China - India rivalry from disrupting rescue operations.

The 18th century founder of modern Nepal, Prithvi Narayan Shah, famously described his new nation as being “like a yam between two boulders.” In his metaphor, China and India were the boulders, and today this dynamic continues to play out in the form of strategic competition for influence in Nepal, which borders both Asian giants.

In the aftermath of the avalanche disaster that triggered a catastrophic flood on August 26 near the Nepal-China border, Kathmandu rushed search-and-rescue (SAR) teams into the debris to find as many of the thousands of missing victims as possible. Despite the scale of the national emergency, Nepal initially declined offers of foreign SAR teams, including from both India and China.

Kathmandu had good reason to be cautious. According to a senior Nepali Foreign Ministry official, the government had learned from its experience following the devastating 2015 earthquake, when the influx of foreign rescue teams—and competition among the countries sending them—created significant coordination and management problems.

The 2015 earthquake demonstrated what Kathmandu hopes to avoid this time around. India and China, alongside other major foreign players such as the U.S., rapidly dispatched rescue personnel and substantial humanitarian assistance, but their responses also became another arena for their broader competition for influence in Nepal.

Following the 2015 disaster, New Delhi launched Operation Maitri and deployed military aircraft, helicopters, medical teams, and rescuers, while Beijing mounted what was then one of its largest overseas humanitarian operations. The resulting competition for visibility and goodwill created practical coordination challenges for an already-overstretched Nepali government.

This time around, Nepal has actively sought to manage the foreign SAR presence, probably to prevent competition from undermining coordination or creating the appearance that Kathmandu favors one nation over another. Indian, Chinese, and South Korean tunnel-rescue specialists have operated in coordination with the Nepali Army, while SAR teams from Australia, Malaysia, and the United Arab Emirates have since joined the effort.

Two weeks after the disaster, Nepal has notably not transitioned entirely from rescue to recovery. On September 8, the government said operations were continuing “while hopes of finding survivors remain,” particularly in hydropower tunnels where workers may have survived in air pockets. Four people were rescued alive between September 4 and 5 alone, including two Nepali workers who survived nine days underground and a Chinese national rescued from another tunnel.

Nepalese leaders have long rejected the idea that Kathmandu should choose between its giant neighbors. Former Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli once put it plainly: “There is no question about aligning with the one or the other. We cannot do it and it is not a viable policy option either.”

Foreign Minister Khanal continued Kathmandu’s tradition of nonaligned foreign policy by noting that “We are effortful to maintain a balanced relationship with all friendly countries, including neighbors India and China.”

Indeed, within his first 100 days in office, Nepal’s current prime minister, Balendra Shah, had been so cautious on this matter that he created a self-imposed rule that while his government could meet individually with diplomatic envoys, it then had to avoid the appearance of favoritism by meeting with the rival ambassador on the same day. Although Shah’s policy of symbolic balance eventually broke down over the summer, Shah’s attempt is a testament to the seriousness with which Nepal takes its nonalignment.

As Nepal’s disaster response has clearly demonstrated, it is not fundamentally opposed to foreign support. Rather, Kathmandu seeks to benefit from foreign support solely on its own terms to avoid unnecessarily antagonizing any partner.

Depending on the circumstances, Nepal could serve as a model on how to deal with intensifying China-India competition for other nations, not just within South Asia, but across the Global South, for years to come. Nepal may remain a yam between two boulders, but Kathmandu is demonstrating that it can still determine how much those boulders shape its fate.

An MP has accused the government of failing to help one of his constituents who has been missing since a deadly flood struck Nepal last month.

Ashington and Blyth MP Ian Lavery told parliament the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) has refused to directly assist in the hunt for Newbiggin-by-the-Sea resident Anirban Battacharyya who, despite living in the UK for 60 years, maintains Indian citizenship.

Lavery asked for urgent talks on how the government "can be more helpful to people who have lived in this country all their lives" but don't have citizenship.

Anthropic said Thursday it shut down multiple cases of state-sponsored surveillance operations that used its artificial intelligence (AI) models, and warned that governments and state-aligned actors are increasingly using AI to spy on ethnic minorities and dissidents.

The incidents were found and disrupted between January and July, and they originated in China, Iran and west Africa, Anthropic said in a report about misuse of its models.

These surveillance campaigns "targeted the same diaspora and dissident communities these regimes have historically targeted. These include pro-democracy figures in Hong Kong, Tibetan and Falun Gong communities across Asia, and Iranian minority communities and opponents of the Iranian regime abroad," the report said.

In one case, Iranian actors developed a way to identify people through their social media accounts; in another, a contractor working for Malian national security authorities used Claude "to design the underlying software that enabled the intelligence gathering."

"AI is now being used in place of an engineering workforce," the report said.

Anthropic also disrupted efforts by users to design weapons, conduct questionable biological research, and create dating scams.

The San Francisco-based AI lab also accused Chinese developers of deceptively using Claude to produce responses to user queries while simultaneously "distilling" that data to improve their own models.

Distilling is an industry term that refers to a process where one AI model is used to train another one.

Chinese developers have previously been accused of using that technique without permission, essentially stealing resources from American labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI.

Now Anthropic alleges that China's Moonshot and DeepSeek have also secretly used Claude to generate answers given to its users.

"In one instance, over a ten-day period, Moonshot relayed almost 300,000 customer requests to Anthropic" through a "network of 5,380 fraudulent accounts, most of which appeared to be located in Singapore and Japan," the report said.

Some of that data contained sensitive user information, potentially in violation of privacy agreements.

"We do not know if Moonshot notified their customers that their requests were being rerouted to Anthropic and exposed to a third party," the report said.

DeepSeek used similar techniques.

When it comes to the research Anthropic detected and blocked that was related to biological weapons, the intent of the actors was less clear-cut and the AI lab did not identify them.

"The individuals implicated in these case studies are working scientists. We do not assert that they intended harm, and identifying them or their labs could expose them to harm," the report said.

The scientific research in those cases involved work around the mosquito-born chikungunya virus, a "highly-pathogenic" strain of the bird flu, a family of viruses that include smallpox and mpox, venoms and other toxins.
